name: Hawthorn
description: Hawthorn is the tree of May, its white blossom foaming over hedgerows at Beltane with a heady, musky scent. In Celtic lands a lone hawthorn standing in a field is a fairy thorn, a doorway to the Otherworld that no sensible farmer would ever cut. Its blood-red haws ripen in autumn and feed the birds through winter, and it has guarded boundaries as living hedges for over a thousand years.
metaphysicalUses: Hawthorn is a guardian and a threshold plant. Its thorns ward against harm and are used in protective witch bottles and poppets, while its blossom is gathered on May morning for fertility, love and marriage magic; in old times brides wore hawthorn crowns. It is sacred to the fair folk, and offerings left beneath a solitary thorn can open contact with faery, though one should never fell such a tree or bring the blossom indoors without asking. Hawthorn is also called on to heal a broken or grieving heart, encouraging the heart to open again, and to bring happiness to a downhearted home. Its wood was used for wands of protection and for the maypole itself.
medicalUses: Hawthorn is one of the most valued heart herbs of Western folk medicine. The flowering tops and berries have long been taken as a tea, tincture or syrup to support the heart and circulation, gently steady the pulse and help maintain healthy blood pressure, and to ease the emotional heaviness and palpitations that come with stress and grief. Herbalists regard it as a slow, nourishing tonic used over weeks or months rather than a quick remedy. The haws were also made into jellies and wines.
whereToFind: Native to Europe, North Africa and western Asia, and naturalized in North America; common in hedgerows, woodland edges, scrub and old pasture. Gather blossoms on a dry morning in May and haws when deep red in September to October, leaving plenty for birds. Easy to grow as a hedge or small tree. Dried berries, leaf and flower are sold by herbal apothecaries and online herb suppliers.
uses: Weave a May crown of hawthorn blossom for Beltane love and fertility rites
Add three thorns to a witch bottle buried at your boundary for protection
Leave milk, honey or bread beneath a lone hawthorn as an offering to the fair folk
Brew a tea of dried flowers and leaves to soothe a grieving heart
Carry dried haws in a red pouch to lift melancholy and invite happiness
Plant a hawthorn hedge to guard your land and home
Simmer haws into a syrup or jelly for autumn kitchen magic
caution: May strengthen the effects of heart and blood pressure medicines; do not combine with nitrates or erectile dysfunction drugs (PDE5 inhibitors), and use with digoxin, beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers only under your doctor's supervision. It should never replace prescribed heart treatment. Can cause dizziness, nausea or palpitations, and too much may drop blood pressure. Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding. The seeds inside the haws contain cyanogenic compounds and should not be crushed or eaten.
interactions: Do not take with nitrates (nitroglycerin, isosorbide) or PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil), as blood pressure may fall too far. May increase the effects of digoxin, beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers, and may add to the effect of blood thinners.

name: Rowan
description: Rowan is the slender tree of the high places, bearing clusters of scarlet berries each marked with a tiny five-pointed star at its base. Across Scotland, Scandinavia and the British Isles it was planted by doors and in churchyards as the foremost charm against witchcraft, the evil eye and enchantment. In Norse myth it saved Thor from drowning by bending low over a raging river.
metaphysicalUses: The old rhyme says 'rowan tree and red thread put the witches to their speed.' Two rowan twigs bound into an equal-armed cross with red thread is the classic protective charm, hung over doors, barns and cradles or carried in the pocket. Rowan wood is prized for dowsing rods, rune staves and wands, and the berries are strung as necklaces for protection and to heighten psychic sight. It is burned in fires to call spirits, familiars and helpers, and planted near graves to keep the dead peaceful. Rowan is a tree of quickening, kindling inner fire, power and the will to succeed.
medicalUses: In folk tradition the ripe berries, always cooked, were made into a tart jelly eaten with game and into syrups and gargles for sore throats and hoarseness. They are rich in vitamin C and were used as a mild astringent for loose bowels and to stimulate digestion. The bark was occasionally used as an astringent wash.
whereToFind: Native to Europe and northern Asia, thriving on mountainsides, moorland, rocky ground and open woodland, often growing high on crags where no other tree survives; widely planted as an ornamental street and garden tree. Berries ripen in late summer to autumn. Saplings are sold at garden centers and nurseries; dried berries are available from some herb suppliers.
uses: Bind two rowan twigs into an equal-armed cross with red thread and hang it over your door
String dried rowan berries on red thread as a protective necklace or altar garland
Carve runes or a wand from fallen rowan wood for protection and divination
Carry a rowan sprig on journeys to ward off ill-wishing
Burn a little rowan wood at Imbolc to honor Brigid and kindle inspiration
Plant a rowan tree near the house as a living guardian
Cook ripe berries into a tart jelly for hearth magic
caution: Raw (fresh) berries contain parasorbic acid and in larger amounts can cause stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and possible kidney damage; eat them only cooked (as in jelly), in modest amounts. Seeds should not be crushed or eaten. Avoid rowan berry remedies in pregnancy and breastfeeding, and ask a healthcare provider first if you have kidney disease.
pets: Keep pets from eating quantities of the berries; they can upset pets' stomachs.

name: Oak
description: Oak is the king of the forest, a tree that can live a thousand years and is said to attract lightning more than any other. It was the holy tree of the Druids, whose very name is thought to share a root with the word for oak, and sacred to sky and thunder gods from Greece to Scandinavia. Mistletoe growing upon oak was the most revered plant of all.
metaphysicalUses: Carry an acorn for luck, youthfulness, longevity and fertility; acorns placed on windowsills were said to keep lightning from striking the house. Oak leaves and bark are used in protection and strength spells, and an oak wand or staff is a powerful tool for drawing down solar and sky energy. Two oak twigs bound with red thread into an equal-armed cross make a protective charm, and gathering an acorn at night was said to help a woman conceive. Oak is a tree of steadfastness and ancient wisdom; meditating against its trunk grounds and strengthens the spirit, and oak is honored at Midsummer and Yule as the Oak King.
medicalUses: Oak bark is strongly astringent with tannins and has traditionally been used as a decoction for gargles and mouthwashes for sore throats, bleeding gums and mouth ulcers, as a wash for minor wounds, weeping skin, sweaty feet and haemorrhoids, and occasionally taken in small amounts for diarrhea (for no more than 3 days). Oak galls were used similarly and to make ink. Acorns, once leached of their bitter tannins, were ground into flour in hard times.
whereToFind: English oak is native to Europe and western Asia, with hundreds of other oak species across the Northern Hemisphere including many in North America; found in woodlands, parks, hedgerows and old estates. Gather fallen acorns and leaves in autumn, and bark only from fallen branches or pruned wood, never by stripping a living tree. Dried oak bark is sold by herb apothecaries.
uses: Carry an acorn in your pocket for luck, strength and longevity
Set acorns on the windowsill to protect the home from storms
Make a staff or wand from fallen oak for solar and sky magic
Burn oak leaves with incense for purification and strength
Decoct oak bark as a gargle for sore throat (external, spit out)
Gild acorns or leaves with gold paint as Yule and Midsummer altar decorations
Sit with your back against an old oak to ground and gather inner strength
caution: Oak bark is very high in tannins. Take it internally for diarrhea for no more than 3 days, and see a doctor for diarrhea that persists, recurs or contains blood; it is not recommended for anyone under 18 or in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Limit external washes, gargles and baths to 1 week, and do not use baths over open wounds, large areas of broken skin or skin infections; avoid hot full baths with fever, heart failure or high blood pressure. Avoid internal use with kidney or liver disease. Raw acorns are bitter and can upset the stomach; they must be leached before eating.
interactions: Tannins can delay or reduce absorption of other medicines and minerals; take oak bark at least 1 hour apart from any medication.
pets: Acorns and oak leaves can cause vomiting and, in large amounts, kidney damage in dogs and horses; keep pets from eating them.

name: Willow
description: Willow loves the water's edge, its long pale branches trailing into streams like hair. It is the tree of the moon, of grief and of enchantment, sacred to Hecate and to the goddesses of the underworld; Circe's grove of willows held the dead. Its supple withies have long been woven into baskets and wands, and the old word for witch, 'wicce', is sometimes linked by folk etymology to the bending wicker.
metaphysicalUses: Willow is the classic wood for wands of moon magic, intuition and healing, and its flexible branches are knotted to work wishes: tie a loose knot in a living withy while speaking your desire, and untie it in thanks when the wish comes true. Willow leaves are carried or added to sachets to attract love, burned with sandalwood under the waning moon for spirit contact, and used in healing spells. It is a tree of grief, and mourners once wore willow; sitting beneath one helps release sorrow. Willow wood also forms the binding for traditional besoms, and its branches are used to protect against evil.
medicalUses: Willow bark is the original source of salicin, from which aspirin was later derived. Long before that, folk healers brewed the bark as a decoction to ease pain, headache, fevers, rheumatic aches, joint inflammation and back pain, and chewed twigs for toothache. It acts more slowly and gently than aspirin. The leaves were sometimes used in washes for skin complaints.
whereToFind: White willow is native to Europe and western and central Asia; willows of many species grow throughout the temperate Northern Hemisphere along rivers, streams, ponds, marshes and wet meadows. Bark is harvested in spring from two- to five-year-old pruned branches, never by ringing a trunk. Willow grows readily from cuttings pushed into damp soil. Dried bark is sold in herbal apothecaries.
uses: Tie a loose knot in a living willow withy as you make a wish, and untie it when granted
Cut a willow wand at the full moon for lunar and healing magic
Burn willow bark with sandalwood under the waning moon for spirit contact
Bind your besom bristles with willow withies in the old way
Sit beneath a willow by water to release grief and sorrow
Brew a willow bark decoction for aches, under appropriate guidance
Weave willow into a protective wreath or dreamcatcher hoop
caution: Contains salicylates: do not use if allergic or sensitive to aspirin, if you have asthma, stomach ulcers, kidney disease or bleeding disorders, or if taking blood thinners, NSAIDs or other salicylate medicines. Stop at least 2 weeks before surgery. Never give to children or teenagers (risk of Reye's syndrome; a toddler died of liver failure after willow bark tea with acetaminophen), and avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Consult a healthcare provider before use.
interactions: May increase bleeding with warfarin and other anticoagulants or antiplatelet drugs, and raises the risk of stomach damage and bleeding with aspirin and NSAIDs such as ibuprofen.
pets: Salicylates are especially dangerous to cats; never give willow bark preparations to pets.

name: Birch
description: Birch is the shining white Lady of the Woods, the first tree to colonize bare land after the ice and so the first letter, Beith, of the Ogham alphabet. It is the tree of beginnings, cleansing and birth; Scottish tradition used its twigs to drive out the spirits of the old year and cradles were made from its wood. In spring its rising sap is tapped for a sweet, clear drink.
metaphysicalUses: Birch is the wood of new beginnings: invoke it to start a new venture, cleanse away the past and open fresh paths. Its twigs form the bristles of the witch's besom, used to sweep negativity and stale energy from a space, and at the turn of the year birch twigs were used in ritual 'beating of the bounds' and to chase out evil. Birch is hung over doors and cradles for protection and blessing, used at Beltane as the maypole, and its bark, which peels into papery strips, makes a natural parchment for writing spells, wishes and petitions to burn. Birch is also a tree of purification and exorcism.
medicalUses: Birch leaf tea has a long tradition as a gentle diuretic, used to support the kidneys and bladder and to help clear the body of excess fluid, and was given for rheumatism, gout and stiff joints. Birch bark and leaf were applied as washes and compresses for skin eruptions and aching muscles, and spring birch sap was drunk as a cleansing tonic. Birch tar was historically used on stubborn skin conditions.
whereToFind: Native to Europe and parts of Asia, with paper birch and other species in North America; it springs up on heaths, open woodland, moorland and disturbed ground and loves light, sandy soils. Collect young leaves in late spring, fallen bark and twigs anytime, and sap only in early spring via responsible tapping. Dried birch leaf is available from herbal suppliers.
uses: Bind birch twigs into a besom to sweep negativity from your home
Write a wish or new-moon intention on a strip of naturally shed birch bark and burn it
Hang a birch twig over the door or cradle for blessing and protection
Use a birch wand in rituals of new beginnings and fresh starts
Add birch leaves to a cleansing ritual bath
Sip birch leaf tea as a traditional spring cleansing tonic
Decorate a birch pole with ribbons for a Beltane maypole
caution: Do not use birch leaf if you are allergic to birch pollen, or if you have been told to limit fluids (for example with serious heart or kidney disease); drink plenty of water while using it, and do not give it to children under 12. Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding, and if aspirin-sensitive. Sweet birch essential oil is almost pure methyl salicylate: a teaspoon or less can kill a child, so never swallow it, store it in a child-resistant bottle, and do not use it on skin while taking warfarin. Burn bark wishes only in a fireproof dish, away from anything flammable.
interactions: Sweet birch (methyl salicylate) oil, even on the skin, can greatly raise warfarin's effect and cause bleeding. Birch leaf may add to the effect of diuretics.
pets: Birch and wintergreen essential oils are toxic to cats and dogs; never apply or diffuse them around pets.

name: Mistletoe
description: Mistletoe hangs green and gold in the bare winter crowns of trees, belonging neither to earth nor sky. Pliny wrote that the Druids cut it from the sacred oak with a golden sickle on the sixth night of the moon, catching it in a white cloth so it never touched the ground. In Norse myth an arrow of mistletoe slew the shining god Baldur, after which Frigga made it a plant of peace and love, and so we kiss beneath it.
metaphysicalUses: Mistletoe is a plant of the in-between, potent at the solstices. Hang a sprig above the door to protect the home from lightning, fire, illness and misfortune, and kiss beneath it to bind love and reconciliation; enemies meeting beneath it were bound to lay down their arms. A sprig is kept for a full year and replaced at Yule, the old one burned. Carry a leaf (sealed in a pouch) as an amulet for luck, protection and fertility, place it near the bed for peaceful dreams and beauty, or hang it over a cradle to keep the faery from stealing the child. It is said to open all locks and break enchantments.
medicalUses: Historically mistletoe was called 'All Heal' and was used by physicians for epilepsy, nervous complaints and high blood pressure, and standardized extracts are used under medical supervision in some European cancer clinics. These are clinical preparations only; the plant itself is poisonous and must not be used as a home remedy.
whereToFind: European mistletoe grows across Europe and western Asia as a hemi-parasite on apple, poplar, lime, hawthorn and occasionally oak; American mistletoe (Phoradendron) grows in the eastern and southern United States. It is most visible in winter in bare treetops and old orchards. Bunches are sold at markets, florists and garden centers in December.
uses: Hang a sprig above the front door at Yule to protect the home for the year
Kiss beneath mistletoe to seal love, peace and reconciliation
Burn last year's sprig in the Yule fire and hang a fresh one
Keep a sealed pouch with a mistletoe leaf on the altar for luck and protection
Hang mistletoe high over a nursery doorway (out of reach) as a blessing
Place a sprig in a framed sealed charm or depict it in art for solstice magic
caution: POISONOUS. All parts, especially the berries and leaves, can cause vomiting, diarrhea, blurred vision, slowed heartbeat, low blood pressure and seizures, and teas brewed from it are the most dangerous. Never eat or brew it. Keep sprigs high, away from children and pets, and gather fallen berries promptly; call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) if any is swallowed. Only clinical extracts prescribed by a physician are used medicinally. Never leave a Yule fire unattended.
pets: Toxic to dogs, cats and horses: causes vomiting, diarrhea, breathing difficulty and slow heart rate. Call a vet or the ASPCA poison line if eaten.

name: Holly
description: Holly keeps its glossy, prickled green through the darkest months, bright with red berries when all else is bare. In the old wheel of the year the Holly King rules the waning half from Midsummer to Yule before yielding to the Oak King. Romans gave holly at Saturnalia, and the custom of decking halls with its boughs at midwinter is older than Christmas.
metaphysicalUses: Holly is a warrior's plant of protection. Plant it near the house or hang boughs indoors in winter to guard against lightning, poison, malicious spirits and ill-wishers; holly hung at Yule gives shelter to friendly woodland spirits through the cold. Its prickly leaves are added to protective sachets and witch bottles, and holly water (leaves soaked in spring water under the full moon) is sprinkled on babies and doorways as a blessing. Men traditionally carried holly for luck, and a holly wand serves for protection and courage. Nine holly leaves gathered on a Friday at midnight and wrapped in a white cloth beneath the pillow were said to bring prophetic dreams.
medicalUses: Holly leaves were once used historically in fevers and rheumatism, but holly is not part of safe modern home herbalism. (A different species, yerba mate, Ilex paraguariensis, is the holly used as a beverage.)
whereToFind: European holly is native to western and southern Europe and northwest Africa and naturalized in parts of North America; American holly (Ilex opaca) grows in the eastern United States. Found in oak and beech woods, hedgerows and as an understorey shrub, and widely planted in gardens. Cut boughs in winter with thanks to the tree; sprigs are sold by florists and markets at midwinter.
uses: Deck your hearth and doorways with holly boughs at Yule for protection
Plant a holly hedge around the home as a living ward
Add a few dried holly leaves to a protection sachet or witch bottle
Wrap nine holly leaves in white cloth beneath your pillow for prophetic dreams
Make holly leaf moon water to sprinkle (externally) over thresholds
Use a holly wand for courage and protective workings
Honor the Holly King at Midsummer and Yule with a sprig on the altar
caution: POISONOUS. Holly berries are toxic; eating more than a few (around five or more) can cause vomiting, diarrhea and drowsiness, and children are most at risk. The leaves are also not for ingestion. Never eat or brew holly. Keep berried branches out of reach of children and pets. Spiny leaves can scratch; wear gloves.
pets: Leaves and berries are toxic to dogs, cats and horses (saponins), causing vomiting, diarrhea and lethargy.

name: Ivy
description: Ivy is the evergreen climber that clasps walls, ruins and trees in a dark, glossy embrace, flowering late in autumn when little else blooms. It was sacred to Dionysus, whose followers wore ivy crowns and whose thyrsus was wound with it, and in the carol it partners holly as the feminine to his masculine. Ivy speaks of fidelity, tenacity and the bonds that hold.
metaphysicalUses: Ivy is a plant of binding and fidelity, given to newlyweds and woven into wedding wreaths to keep love faithful and enduring. Grow it up the walls of a house to protect the inhabitants from negativity and disaster, or use a length of vine in cord and knot magic to bind a spell, a friendship or a vow. Carried by women it was said to bring good fortune, and an ivy leaf in a sachet guards against misfortune. Paired with holly at midwinter it represents the union of the feminine and masculine. Ivy is also used in ritual crowns for celebration and ecstatic work in honor of Dionysus.
medicalUses: Standardized ivy leaf extracts are used in some commercial European cough syrups as an expectorant, but raw ivy is irritant and its berries are poisonous, so it is not used as a home remedy.
whereToFind: Native to Europe and western Asia and naturalized (often invasively) in North America and elsewhere; grows on walls, trees, woodland floors, hedges and old buildings in shade. Cut lengths of vine any time of year, wearing gloves. Ivy plants are sold in every garden center.
uses: Weave ivy into a wedding or handfasting wreath for fidelity
Bind a spell by wrapping its token or poppet in an ivy vine
Grow ivy up your house walls as a protective cloak
Pair holly and ivy on the Yule altar to honor masculine and feminine
Wear an ivy crown in celebration rites for Dionysus
Exchange ivy sprigs with a dear friend to seal a lasting friendship
caution: POISONOUS. Ivy berries and leaves are toxic if eaten and can cause vomiting, diarrhea and abdominal pain. Sap and leaves can cause allergic contact dermatitis and blistering in sensitive people; wear gloves when handling and when wearing ivy crowns or wreaths. Never brew or eat raw ivy; only commercial standardized ivy-leaf cough products are taken internally, and they should be avoided in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Keep it away from children and pets. Not related to poison ivy, but still irritant.
pets: Toxic to dogs, cats and horses (the leaves more than the berries), causing vomiting, drooling, abdominal pain and diarrhea.

name: Dandelion
description: The humble dandelion is a little sun in the grass by day and a moon of silver seed by night. Its name comes from the French dent de lion for its jagged, lion-toothed leaves. Scorned as a weed, it is in truth one of the most nourishing and useful plants in the hedge-witch's cupboard, every part edible from root to flower.
metaphysicalUses: Blow the seeds of a dandelion clock while making a wish and the wind will carry it to the spirits; count the breaths needed to clear it to learn the hour, or the years until you marry. Blow the seeds toward a loved one to send them a message. The roasted root is brewed into a tea to heighten psychic powers, and a steaming cup set beside the bed is said to call spirits. Bury dandelion in the northwest corner of the house to bring favorable winds, and use the bright flowers in sun magic, abundance and resilience spells; nothing roots out a dandelion, and it lends that tenacity to your workings.
medicalUses: Dandelion is a classic spring bitter. The leaves, eaten in salads or as tea, are a nourishing traditional diuretic rich in potassium, used to ease water retention and support the kidneys. The root, taken as decoction, tincture or roasted 'coffee', has long been used to support the liver and gallbladder, stimulate digestion and appetite, ease sluggish bowels and clear the skin. The flowers make a cheerful wine and fritters, and the milky sap was dabbed on warts.
whereToFind: Native to Eurasia and now found almost worldwide in lawns, meadows, roadsides, gardens and waste ground. Gather young leaves in early spring before flowering (they grow bitter later), flowers on sunny mornings, and roots in autumn when they are fullest. Forage only from unsprayed ground away from roads. Dried root and leaf are sold by herb shops and health food stores.
uses: Blow a dandelion clock while speaking a wish into the wind
Brew roasted dandelion root tea before divination to open psychic sight
Set a cup of dandelion tea beside your bed to invite helpful spirits
Make dandelion flower honey or wine to bottle summer sunshine
Add young leaves to a spring salad as a cleansing tonic
Bury a dandelion root in the northwest corner of your garden for favorable winds
Press the golden flowers into a jar spell for resilience and abundance
caution: Avoid if allergic to the daisy family (Asteraceae, including ragweed); topical use may trigger reactions in people with eczema. Stick to food amounts in pregnancy and breastfeeding, since higher doses are not proven safe. Consult a healthcare provider if you have gallstones, bile duct obstruction, stomach ulcers, kidney problems or a bleeding disorder, or take medications (see interactions). Very heavy, long-term tea drinking has been linked to high oxalate levels. Sap may irritate sensitive skin. Do not forage from lawns treated with herbicides.
interactions: May add to the effects of diuretics (with high potassium risk alongside potassium-sparing diuretics such as spironolactone), diabetes drugs including insulin, and blood thinners or antiplatelet drugs. May raise lithium levels and reduce absorption of quinolone antibiotics, and may alter levels of drugs processed by CYP1A2 and CYP3A4; a transplant patient developed toxic immunosuppressant levels after dandelion tea.

name: Nettle
description: Nettle defends itself with a thousand tiny stinging hairs, yet beneath its fierce manner lies one of the most nourishing greens in the hedgerow. It was sacred to Thor, and in Hans Christian Andersen's tale a sister wove nettle shirts to break the spell on her swan brothers. Nettle fibre has been spun into cloth since the Bronze Age.
metaphysicalUses: Nettle is a fierce plant for returning a curse to its sender: stuff a poppet with nettle to send back ill-will, or sprinkle it around the home to keep evil out. Carry nettle in a sachet to ward off negativity and danger, or hold it during a crisis to dispel fear and lend courage. Throw nettle into a fire to avert danger, or place a bowl of fresh nettles under a sickbed to aid recovery. It is a key herb in exorcism and banishing blends, and as a Mars herb it also stirs passion and lust. Wearing nettle was said to protect against lightning.
medicalUses: Cooked or dried, nettle loses its sting and becomes a deeply nourishing spring tonic rich in iron, calcium, chlorophyll and vitamins, traditionally taken as tea, soup or pottage to build the blood, restore vitality and support recovery. Folk healers have used it for seasonal allergies and hay fever, as a gentle diuretic, and for arthritis and gout; deliberate 'urtication' with fresh stinging nettle was an old remedy for aching joints. Nettle rinses were used for hair and scalp health, and nettle root is used for prostate support.
whereToFind: Native to Europe, Asia, northern Africa and western North America and naturalized widely; thrives in rich, damp soil near habitation, woodland edges, riverbanks and old farmyards. Harvest the top few pairs of leaves with gloves in spring before flowering (older leaves may irritate the kidneys). Dried leaf is widely available from herbal suppliers and health food stores.
uses: Stuff a poppet with dried nettle to return a curse to its sender
Sprinkle dried nettle across the threshold to keep harm away
Brew a mineral-rich nettle tea as a spring tonic
Cook young nettle tops into a traditional spring soup
Carry nettle in a red pouch for courage in a crisis
Use a cooled nettle infusion as a strengthening hair rinse
Add nettle to uncrossing and banishing incense
caution: Wear gloves when harvesting; fresh nettle stings and can cause hives. Do not eat raw. Avoid in pregnancy (it is a reputed abortifacient) and while breastfeeding, and do not give medicinal amounts to children under 12. Consult a healthcare provider if you have diabetes, low blood pressure or kidney problems, or take the medicines listed under interactions. Use only young leaves gathered before flowering for food.
interactions: Its high vitamin K content can weaken warfarin. May raise lithium levels, add to the effects of diabetes and blood pressure medicines (including diuretics), and add drowsiness with sedatives.

name: Plantain
description: Plantain is the low, ribbed rosette that grows wherever feet tread, so faithfully that Indigenous Americans called it 'white man's foot' for how it followed European settlers. It is Waybread, one of the nine sacred herbs of the Anglo-Saxon Nine Herbs Charm, praised as 'mother of herbs' that withstands carts and the trampling of oxen. It is the first-aid plant of every footpath.
metaphysicalUses: Plantain is a traveler's herb; tuck a leaf into your shoe to prevent weariness on long journeys and to keep you on the right path. Hang it in the car or carry it for protection on the road. As one of the Nine Sacred Herbs it is used to drive away venom, evil and ill-intent, and placed in protective sachets. Its endurance under trampling lends strength and resilience to spells for those who must keep going under pressure. Plantain is also used in healing magic and to draw out negativity as it draws out splinters, and the root was hung around the neck against snakebite and headache.
medicalUses: Plantain is the classic field remedy: a fresh leaf chewed or crushed into a 'spit poultice' and laid on a bee sting, insect bite, nettle sting, splinter or small cut soothes, draws and helps it heal. It is cooling, soothing and gently astringent, made into salves for rashes, burns, chapped skin and minor wounds. The leaf tea was taken for coughs and irritated throats and to soothe the digestive tract, and the seeds (related to psyllium) were used as a gentle bulk laxative.
whereToFind: Native to Europe and Asia and now naturalized almost everywhere; grows in lawns, paths, gravel drives, roadsides and compacted ground. Pick leaves from spring through autumn from clean, unsprayed areas. Narrow-leaf plantain (Plantago lanceolata) is used interchangeably. Dried leaf is sold by herbal suppliers.
uses: Chew a fresh leaf and press it onto a bee sting or bug bite as a spit poultice
Tuck a plantain leaf into your shoe for stamina on a long journey
Infuse plantain in oil and make a healing salve for scrapes and rashes
Hang dried plantain in your car as a travel protection charm
Add plantain to a protection sachet with the other Nine Sacred Herbs
Brew a soothing plantain leaf tea for a tickly cough
caution: Generally very safe for skin use, though plantain creams occasionally cause allergic skin reactions, and the pollen and psyllium seed are known allergens. Medicinal amounts by mouth are considered likely unsafe in pregnancy (it can affect the uterus) and should be avoided while breastfeeding. Plantain seed (psyllium) can reduce absorption of medicines; take it at a different time with plenty of water, and do not use it if you have trouble swallowing or a bowel blockage. Forage only from unsprayed ground.
interactions: The leaves are high in vitamin K and may reduce the effect of warfarin. Seed (psyllium) preparations can lower absorption of lithium, carbamazepine and other medicines and may lower blood sugar, so separate doses by a couple of hours and monitor glucose if you take diabetes medicines.

name: Burdock
description: Burdock is a stately biennial with enormous rhubarb-like leaves and purple thistle flowers that ripen into hooked burrs which cling to every passing coat and dog; they famously inspired the invention of Velcro. Its long taproot is a prized vegetable in Japan called gobo. In folk magic its clinging burrs and deep root speak of protection and cleansing.
metaphysicalUses: Burdock is a protector and purifier. Gather the root in the waning moon, dry it, and string slices on red thread to wear or hang as an amulet against negativity and evil. Burn the dried root in protective and purifying incense, or sprinkle it around the home to banish unwanted energies. The burrs, which cling to whatever passes, are used in hoodoo to 'stick' an intention or keep someone near, and in counter-magic to catch and hold harm before it reaches you. Burdock is also added to healing and uncrossing baths and some love sachets.
medicalUses: Burdock root is one of the great 'blood purifiers' or alteratives of folk herbalism, taken as a decoction, tincture or simply eaten as a vegetable to support the liver, kidneys and lymph, to nourish digestion as a source of inulin, and especially to clear chronic skin troubles such as acne, eczema and boils. It has been paired with dandelion in traditional cleansing drinks for centuries. The leaves were used as poultices for burns, sores and swellings.
whereToFind: Native to Europe and Asia and naturalized across North America; grows in waste ground, field edges, hedgerows, riverbanks and disturbed soil. Dig the root in the autumn of the first year or spring of the second, before the flower stalk rises; it runs deep, so bring a spade. Fresh gobo is sold in Asian groceries; dried root from herb apothecaries.
uses: String dried burdock root slices on red thread as a protective amulet
Burn powdered root in a purification and banishing incense
Hide a burdock burr in a doorway to catch harm before it enters
Simmer burdock root in a cleansing broth or stir-fry
Brew a decoction of root as a traditional skin-clearing tonic
Add burdock to an uncrossing bath with hyssop and salt
caution: Avoid in pregnancy (it may stimulate the uterus) and breastfeeding. May lower blood sugar and slow blood clotting; consult a healthcare provider if you have diabetes or a bleeding disorder or take related medicines, and stop at least 2 weeks before surgery. Avoid if allergic to the daisy family, including chrysanthemums. Some commercial burdock teas have been contaminated with belladonna (atropine), so buy only from reputable sources. When foraging, the young plant can resemble poisonous foxglove; identify with certainty. Burrs can irritate skin.
interactions: May add to the effects of diabetes medicines (risk of low blood sugar) and of blood thinners and antiplatelet drugs such as warfarin, aspirin and NSAIDs (risk of bleeding).

name: Comfrey
description: Comfrey is a lush, bristly plant with drooping bells of purple, cream or pink, beloved by bees and gardeners alike. Its old names, knitbone and boneset, and its Latin Symphytum, from the Greek for 'to unite', all tell of its legendary power to knit broken bones and torn flesh. Gardeners prize it as a deep-rooted dynamic accumulator and compost activator.
metaphysicalUses: Comfrey is the traveler's guardian: wear or carry a leaf, or tuck one into your luggage, to keep you and your belongings safe on journeys and to prevent theft. Some put a piece of root in the car glovebox. Comfrey root is also added to money spells, wrapped around coins or stored with cash to keep it from leaving and to make it return, and it is used in healing magic to help mend what is broken, in body, relationship or circumstance. As a Saturn herb it lends stability and endurance to workings.
medicalUses: Comfrey has been applied externally for centuries as a poultice, compress, infused oil or salve for bruises, sprains, strains, swollen joints, aching muscles and closed fractures, and traditionally to help heal sores and ulcers. It contains allantoin, which encourages cell regeneration. Modern herbalists use it only externally on unbroken skin because of the liver-toxic alkaloids it contains; historical internal use is no longer considered safe.
whereToFind: Native to Europe and western Asia and naturalized in North America; grows in damp meadows, ditches, riverbanks and field margins, and is widely cultivated in herb and permaculture gardens ('Russian comfrey' Bocking 14 is a sterile variety that won't spread). Harvest leaves from late spring through summer. Dried leaf and comfrey salves are sold by herbalists.
uses: Tuck a comfrey leaf in your suitcase to keep it safe while traveling
Wrap a piece of comfrey root around a coin in your wallet to keep money returning
Make a comfrey-infused oil or salve for bruises and sprains (external only)
Lay a fresh-leaf poultice over a strained muscle or swollen ankle
Use comfrey in healing spells to mend what is broken
Steep leaves in water for a rich 'comfrey tea' fertilizer for the garden
caution: EXTERNAL USE ONLY. Comfrey contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids that can cause serious, sometimes fatal liver damage (veno-occlusive disease) and may cause cancer if taken internally; do not eat or drink it, and the FDA has advised removing oral comfrey products from the market. The alkaloids are also absorbed through skin, so use it only on unbroken skin, never on open or deep wounds, in small amounts, and for less than 10 days at a time. The root holds far more alkaloids than the leaf. Avoid entirely, even on the skin, in pregnancy, breastfeeding, liver or kidney disease and on infants and young children. Young leaves can be mistaken for poisonous foxglove.
interactions: Do not combine with medicines that can harm the liver (such as acetaminophen, methotrexate, amiodarone or statins). Drugs that induce liver enzymes (such as phenobarbital, carbamazepine, phenytoin or rifampin) can make the alkaloids more toxic.
pets: Keep away from pets and livestock; the alkaloids damage animals' livers too.

name: Mullein
description: Mullein rises from a rosette of soft, silvery-velvet leaves into a tall spike studded with sulphur-yellow flowers, standing like a candle in waste places. The dried stalks were dipped in tallow and burned as torches, earning the names Hag's Taper and Witch's Candle. In Greek myth Hermes gave Ulysses mullein to guard him against Circe's enchantments.
metaphysicalUses: Mullein is a premier protection and courage herb. Carry the leaves to keep wild animals at bay and to give courage, tuck them in your shoes to protect you on the road, or sew them into a dream pillow to guard against nightmares. Powdered mullein leaf is the traditional substitute for graveyard dirt when graveyard soil cannot be obtained, and it is used in necromancy and spirit work. The dried stalk, dipped in wax or tallow, becomes a ritual torch or candle for invoking spirits and honoring the dead, and a sprig hung over the door keeps away evil. An old Ozark love divination involved bending a mullein stalk toward a lover's house and watching whether it rose again.
medicalUses: Mullein leaf is a time-honored remedy for the lungs: a tea or syrup of the soft leaves soothes dry, irritating coughs, loosens congestion and eases chest colds, bronchitis and sore throats, and the leaves were even smoked for asthma in the past. Mullein flowers infused in olive oil, often with garlic, make the classic folk ear oil for earache in an intact eardrum. The leaves were also laid on as soothing poultices for skin sores and inflammation.
whereToFind: Native to Europe, North Africa and Asia and naturalized throughout North America; grows in dry, sunny, disturbed places such as roadsides, railway embankments, gravel pits, field edges and burned ground. Gather leaves from the first-year rosette or before flowering, and pick flowers individually through summer. Dried leaf is sold by herbal apothecaries and online.
uses: Dip a dried mullein stalk in beeswax to make a Hag's Taper for rituals
Use powdered mullein leaf as a substitute for graveyard dirt in spell work
Tuck a leaf in your shoe for protection and courage on journeys
Sew mullein into a dream pillow to banish nightmares
Brew mullein leaf tea, strained through fine cloth, for a dry cough
Infuse the golden flowers in olive oil for a traditional ear oil
Hang a sprig over the door to keep evil away
caution: The fine leaf hairs can irritate the throat and skin; always strain mullein tea through a coffee filter or fine cloth. Contact dermatitis has been reported from handling the plant. Never put ear oil into an ear with a perforated eardrum, discharge or tubes; see a healthcare provider for ear pain in children. The seeds may be toxic and must not be eaten. Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding, as safety is not established.
interactions: No known interactions; ask a healthcare provider if you take medicines.

name: Red Clover
description: Red clover fills summer meadows with its rosy-purple globes, sweet with nectar and humming with bees. Its threefold leaf has been revered as a symbol of the triple goddess and later of the Trinity, and finding a rare four-leaved clover is one of the oldest luck charms in the world. Farmers sowed it to enrich their soil, for it fixes nitrogen from the air.
metaphysicalUses: Red clover is a luck and prosperity plant. Carry a leaf or flower for good fortune, add it to money and success spells, and sprinkle its infusion around a property to remove negative spirits. Two-leaved clover found and carried brings a lover; three-leaved is worn as protection; four-leaved helps one see the fair folk and resist enchantment; five-leaved brings wealth. Red clover in the bathwater helps with financial arrangements, and it is used in rituals of fidelity, love and blessing for animals and livestock. A clover infusion poured as a floor wash clears away unwanted spirits.
medicalUses: The flower heads have long been brewed as a gentle tea and syrup for spasmodic coughs and bronchitis, and red clover is a classic folk 'blood cleanser' or alterative used for chronic skin conditions like eczema and psoriasis and to support the lymphatic system. It contains plant isoflavones and is used by some women for menopausal symptoms such as hot flashes. Salves and washes of the flowers were applied to sores and skin complaints.
whereToFind: Native to Europe, western Asia and northwest Africa and naturalized throughout North America; grows in meadows, pastures, lawns, roadsides and field edges. Gather fresh, bright flower heads on a dry summer morning, discarding any that are brown, and dry them quickly. Dried blossoms are sold by herbal suppliers.
uses: Carry a pressed four-leaved clover in your wallet for luck
Add red clover blossoms to a money-drawing sachet or jar
Sprinkle a red clover infusion across the property to clear unwanted spirits
Brew a gentle blossom tea or syrup for a spasmodic cough
Add blossoms to a ritual bath before signing financial agreements
Wear a three-leaved clover as a protective charm
caution: Contains phytoestrogens; avoid medicinal amounts (and skin use) in pregnancy and breastfeeding and with hormone-sensitive conditions such as breast, uterine or ovarian cancer, endometriosis or fibroids. Do not take with tamoxifen or hormone therapy, and do not give to children under 12. May slow blood clotting; avoid with bleeding disorders or protein S deficiency, use caution with blood thinners, and stop two weeks before surgery. Discard any moldy flowers.
interactions: Do not take with tamoxifen; may reduce the effect of estrogen medicines and birth control pills (use backup contraception). May increase bleeding with anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs (warfarin, aspirin, heparin), may slow breakdown of drugs processed by CYP1A2, 2C9, 2C19 and 3A4, and has been linked to methotrexate toxicity in one case.

name: Echinacea
description: Echinacea is a North American prairie native whose drooping magenta petals surround a spiny, copper-orange cone; its name comes from echinos, the Greek for hedgehog. It was one of the most widely used medicines of the Plains nations, who used it for snakebite, wounds and infections, and it became a pillar of 19th-century American Eclectic medicine. Butterflies and finches adore it.
metaphysicalUses: Echinacea is used to strengthen spells, offered to spirits and to the Earth, and added to workings to amplify their power and to bring stamina, prosperity and inner strength. It is a natural herb of healing magic, especially for building resilience against illness and for defending your energy field. Planting coneflowers around the home is said to draw prosperity and good health, and the spiny cone is used in protection charms to deter ill will, like the hedgehog it is named for.
medicalUses: Echinacea is one of the most popular immune herbs in the world. Taken as a tincture or tea at the very first sign of a cold, flu or sore throat, it is traditionally used to rouse the body's defenses and shorten illness. The root tincture causes a characteristic tingling of the tongue. Plains peoples applied the root to wounds, burns, insect stings and snakebite and chewed it for toothache and sore throat. It is best used in short courses rather than continuously.
whereToFind: Native to the prairies, open woods and meadows of central and eastern North America; wild populations are now at risk from overharvest, so grow your own or buy cultivated stock. It thrives in sunny, well-drained garden beds and is sold at nearly every garden center. Harvest flowers in summer and roots from plants three years or older in autumn. Dried root, herb and tinctures are sold by apothecaries and health stores.
uses: Plant coneflowers around your home to draw health and prosperity
Add dried echinacea to any spell to strengthen and empower it
Offer dried petals to the Earth or the spirits in thanks
Take echinacea tincture at the first tickle of a cold
Carry a dried cone in a protection pouch to guard your energy
Brew a tea of root and flowers during winter cold season
caution: Avoid if allergic to the daisy family (ragweed, chrysanthemums, marigolds) or if you are prone to allergies or asthma; reactions can be severe. Avoid with autoimmune conditions (such as lupus, rheumatoid arthritis or MS), and consult a healthcare provider if you have tuberculosis or HIV, take immunosuppressants, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or are giving it to a child (rashes have occurred in children). Use in short courses (about 7-10 days). Seek medical advice for persistent infection. Buy only cultivated echinacea; wild plants are at risk.
interactions: May reduce the effect of immunosuppressant drugs (such as those used after transplants). May raise caffeine levels and alter drugs processed by CYP3A4 and CYP1A2 liver enzymes.

name: Elecampane
description: Elecampane is a towering, sun-yellow daisy with huge leaves and a fragrant, aromatic root. Legend says it sprang from the tears of Helen of Troy as she was carried away, giving it the name helenium, and in the Saxon lands it was elfwort, the herb used against elf-shot, the invisible arrows of the faery that brought sudden illness. Candied elecampane root was once sold as a sweetmeat for the lungs.
metaphysicalUses: As elfwort, elecampane is used both to attract and to protect against the fair folk. Grow it in the garden or leave it as an offering to befriend them, or carry it to ward off elf-shot and faery mischief. Sew the leaves into a pink or red cloth and carry them, or burn the root, to attract love. Burned on charcoal it is said to sharpen psychic powers, especially when scrying, and it is added to incense for divination. Elecampane is also used in protective sachets and in healing spells, particularly for the chest and breath.
medicalUses: Elecampane root is a warming, aromatic lung herb used for centuries as a syrup, decoction, honey or candied root for stubborn, wet coughs, bronchitis and chest colds, helping to loosen and bring up mucus. It is rich in inulin and bitter compounds and was also taken as a digestive tonic to stimulate appetite and settle a sluggish stomach. Horse-heal, its old name, came from its use in veterinary medicine.
whereToFind: Native to central Asia and southern and central Europe and naturalized in parts of Britain and eastern North America in damp meadows, field edges and roadsides; most often found in old herb gardens. Easy to grow in moist, sunny ground. Dig roots from second- or third-year plants in autumn. Dried root is available from herbal apothecaries.
uses: Plant elecampane in the garden as an offering to the fair folk
Burn a pinch of powdered root on charcoal before scrying
Sew elecampane leaves into a pink cloth and carry to attract love
Make elecampane-infused honey or syrup for a wet cough
Carry the root in a sachet to guard against elf-shot and mischief
Candy slices of root in sugar syrup as an old-fashioned lozenge
caution: Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding. May cause allergic reactions in those sensitive to the daisy family (Asteraceae, including ragweed and chamomile), and contact dermatitis from handling. Large doses can cause vomiting, diarrhea, cramps and even paralysis-like symptoms. May affect blood sugar and blood pressure and cause drowsiness; consult a healthcare provider if taking medications and stop 2 weeks before surgery. Not for young children. Burn root on charcoal only in a well-ventilated room, in a heatproof dish.
interactions: May increase drowsiness with sedatives such as benzodiazepines, barbiturates and sleep medicines, and may interfere with diabetes and blood pressure medicines.

name: Angelica
description: Angelica is a magnificent, tall umbellifer with great globes of greenish-white flowers and hollow, fragrant stems. Legend tells that the Archangel Michael revealed it to a monk in a dream as a cure for the plague, and it blooms around his feast day in the old calendar, hence its name. Its candied green stems decorate cakes, and its root flavors gin, Chartreuse and Benedictine.
metaphysicalUses: Angelica is one of the most powerful herbs of protection and is said to be guarded by angels. Grow it in the garden as a guardian, carry the root as an amulet, or sprinkle dried angelica in the four corners of the house to ward off evil. Burn the dried leaves in exorcism rites, and add the herb to the bath to remove curses, hexes and spells cast against you. In hoodoo, angelica root is carried by women as a protector of women and children and for luck. Smoking or burning it was said to bring visions, and it is used in rituals invoking angelic protection and healing.
medicalUses: Angelica root is a warming, aromatic bitter used in European folk medicine to stimulate appetite and digestion, ease gas, bloating and indigestion, and warm cold hands and feet. It was taken in teas and cordials for colds, coughs and bronchitis to warm the chest and loosen phlegm, and for menstrual cramps. It was famously a component of plague remedies such as the 'Carmelite water'.
whereToFind: Native to northern Europe, Scandinavia, Iceland, Greenland and Russia, growing in damp meadows, riverbanks and mountain streamsides; widely grown in herb gardens. Sow fresh seed in autumn in rich, moist soil. Harvest roots in the autumn of the first year and stems in spring. Dried root is sold by apothecaries and hoodoo supply shops. Be certain of identification: it resembles deadly water hemlock.
uses: Sprinkle dried angelica in the four corners of the house to ward off evil
Carry a piece of angelica root as an amulet for women and children
Add angelica to an uncrossing bath with hyssop and rue
Burn dried leaves in exorcism or house-clearing rites
Grow angelica in the garden as an angelic guardian plant
Candy the young stems for a festive, protective sweet
Sip a mild angelica root tea after a heavy meal for digestion
caution: Avoid in pregnancy (it can stimulate the uterus and menstruation) and breastfeeding. Contains furanocoumarins that cause photosensitivity and burns; avoid sun exposure for 12-18 hours after skin contact or baths, and handle the fresh plant with gloves (rue, often paired with it in baths, adds to this risk). Do not take the essential oil internally. May interact with blood thinners; consult a healthcare provider. Never forage wild angelica unless expert: it is easily confused with deadly water hemlock and poison hemlock. Burn leaves only in a heatproof dish with good ventilation.
interactions: May increase bleeding risk with warfarin and other blood thinners (related angelica species have antiplatelet effects).

name: Lovage
description: Lovage is a tall, glossy, celery-scented giant of the old cottage garden, its taste so savory that Germans call it Maggikraut. The Romans carried it across Europe as a culinary herb, and medieval travelers stuffed its leaves in their shoes to refresh weary feet. Its very name, though in truth derived from 'Ligusticum', has made it a beloved herb of love magic.
metaphysicalUses: Lovage is a classic herb of love and allure. Add it to a ritual bath (in a sachet or as an infusion) before meeting a new person or going out, to make yourself more attractive and loveable. Carry lovage root or leaves in a pouch to draw love, or include it in love sachets and charms. It is also used in glamour and beauty spells, and like its old use in travelers' shoes, it can be tucked into footwear to ease and protect long journeys.
medicalUses: Lovage has been used in European folk medicine as a warming digestive, eaten or taken as tea to ease gas, bloating and indigestion and to stimulate appetite. The root and seed were traditionally used as a diuretic to flush the urinary tract and kidneys and reduce fluid retention, and a gargle of leaves was used for sore throats and mouth ulcers. Its leaves and stems are eaten like celery in soups and stews.
whereToFind: Native to southern and eastern Europe and southwestern Asia; cultivated in herb and kitchen gardens across temperate regions and occasionally escaping to roadsides. A hardy perennial that thrives in rich, moist soil and returns each year, growing up to two meters. Plants are sold at herb nurseries and garden centers; dried leaf and root from herb suppliers.
uses: Add a lovage sachet to your bath before a date to become more attractive
Carry dried lovage root in a red pouch to draw love
Tuck a lovage leaf in your shoes for a comfortable journey
Add fresh leaves to soups and stews in kitchen love magic
Include lovage in a self-love and glamour jar
Sip a cup of lovage leaf tea after meals to ease bloating
caution: Avoid in pregnancy (it may trigger uterine contractions or menstruation) and while breastfeeding. Avoid with kidney inflammation or impaired kidney function, and do not use it with large amounts of fluid if you have fluid retention from heart or kidney disease. It may raise sodium levels and blood pressure. Handling the fresh plant in sunlight can cause blistering skin reactions, and regular use may increase sun sensitivity; wear gloves when harvesting. Avoid if allergic to celery or other Apiaceae plants, and do not confuse it with poisonous water dropwort (Oenanthe).
interactions: Acts like a water pill, so combining it with diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide, furosemide) may cause excess fluid loss, dizziness and low blood pressure. Root coumarins may increase bleeding with warfarin and other anticoagulants.

name: Fennel
description: Fennel is a graceful, feathery umbellifer with golden flower heads and a sweet anise scent. In Greek myth Prometheus stole fire from the gods hidden inside a hollow fennel stalk, and Dionysus' thyrsus was made of giant fennel. It was one of the nine sacred herbs of the Anglo-Saxons, and medieval households hung it over doors on Midsummer's Eve against evil spirits.
metaphysicalUses: Fennel is a protective herb hung in windows and over doors, especially at Midsummer, to keep evil spirits and unwanted visitors away, and a little fennel seed in the keyhole was said to keep ghosts out. Carry fennel for courage, strength and long life, and add it to healing and purification sachets. It is used in spells for vitality and to lend persuasive, clear speech. In the old days fennel seeds were chewed in church to stave off hunger and were thought to give strength and keep the soul from temptation.
medicalUses: Fennel seed is one of the gentlest and most widely used digestive herbs; chewed after meals or brewed as a tea, it eases gas, bloating, cramping and indigestion and freshens the breath. Fennel tea has long been given in small amounts for infant colic and taken by nursing mothers to encourage milk flow, though current European guidance advises against it for children under 4 and during pregnancy and breastfeeding. It was also used as a soothing expectorant for coughs, and fennel water as an eyewash for tired eyes.
whereToFind: Native to the Mediterranean and naturalized across many temperate regions, including California and Australia, where it grows wild on roadsides, coastal bluffs and waste ground. Easy to grow in sunny, well-drained garden beds. Harvest leaves through summer and seeds when they turn brown in late summer to autumn. Seeds are sold in every grocery spice aisle; bulb fennel in produce sections.
uses: Hang fennel over your door at Midsummer to keep evil spirits away
Place a few fennel seeds in a keyhole to keep ghosts out
Chew a pinch of fennel seed after meals to ease digestion and sweeten the breath
Carry fennel seeds in a pouch for courage and strength
Brew fennel seed tea for gas and bloating
Add fennel to a protective and purifying ritual bath
Cook with fennel bulb in kitchen magic for vitality and long life
caution: Generally safe in culinary amounts. European regulators advise against fennel tea for children under 4 without a pediatrician's advice, and against medicinal use in pregnancy and breastfeeding, partly because it contains estragole. Avoid medicinal doses with estrogen-sensitive conditions. Fennel essential oil must not be taken internally or used on young children. Avoid if allergic to celery, carrot, dill, caraway, aniseed or mugwort. Never forage wild umbellifers without certain identification, as hemlock looks similar.
interactions: Estrogen-like compounds may interfere with hormone therapy or birth control in medicinal doses.

name: Dill
description: Dill is a slender, airy annual with thread-fine blue-green leaves and flat yellow umbels. Its name comes from the Old Norse dilla, 'to lull', for dill water was given to soothe crying babies. In medieval Europe it was hung over cradles and doorways to thwart witches and envious eyes, while the witches themselves were said to use it in their own charms.
metaphysicalUses: Dill is a protective herb hung over doors and above cradles to guard the household and children, and carried in a pouch over the heart to protect against the evil eye. Its abundant seeds make it a money herb: place dill seed in your wallet or purse to draw money, or add it to prosperity sachets. Dill in the bath makes one irresistible to a lover, and eating dill or adding it to food stirs lust. An old rhyme bids brides tuck dill and salt in their shoes for luck. Dill also lends a gentle, lulling energy to spells for peace and calm in the home.
medicalUses: Dill seed is a soothing carminative, chewed or brewed as tea to relieve gas, bloating, hiccups, indigestion and mild nausea, and the classic gripe water given to colicky babies has long contained dill. Its lulling reputation came from use as a mild calming tea for restlessness and sleep. Nursing mothers drank dill seed tea to encourage milk, and chewing the seeds sweetened the breath.
whereToFind: Native to southwest Asia and the eastern Mediterranean; grown in kitchen gardens worldwide and occasionally naturalized in fields. Sow directly in sunny ground in spring; it bolts quickly in heat, so sow successively. Harvest leaves before flowering and seeds when brown. Fresh and dried dill weed and seed are sold in every grocery store.
uses: Hang a bundle of dried dill above the front door for protection
Keep a few dill seeds in your wallet to draw money
Add dill to a love bath to make yourself irresistible
Tuck dill and salt into a bride's shoe for wedding luck
Brew dill seed tea for gas and bloating
Season food with fresh dill in kitchen magic for luck and lust
Place a sachet of dill near a cradle (out of reach) for a peaceful child
caution: Safe in culinary amounts. Avoid medicinal doses in pregnancy (seeds may stimulate menstruation) and stick to food amounts while breastfeeding. Fresh dill juice may cause sun sensitivity, and dill on the skin can irritate. Avoid if allergic to carrot-family plants such as fennel, celery, coriander or caraway. Dill extract may lower blood sugar; stop medicinal use 2 weeks before surgery, and consult a healthcare provider before giving remedies to infants or if taking lithium or diabetes medication.
interactions: May lower blood sugar with diabetes medicines (insulin, glyburide, metformin) and, as a mild diuretic, may raise lithium levels.

name: Caraway
description: Caraway is a biennial umbellifer whose crescent-shaped, ribbed seeds have flavored rye bread, sauerkraut and seed cake for thousands of years; seeds have been found in Stone Age lake dwellings in Switzerland. Folk belief held that caraway could keep anything from being stolen and anyone from straying, so it was fed to homing pigeons and given to lovers. It was a staple of medieval love potions.
metaphysicalUses: Caraway is the herb of keeping: it is said to prevent theft of whatever it is kept with, so a few seeds are placed in boxes, purses and cars to guard belongings. It was baked into cakes and breads or fed to a lover to keep them faithful and to attract a mate, and it is added to love sachets for lust and fidelity. Carry caraway to protect against negative entities and Lilith-type spirits; it was placed in children's beds to guard them. Chewing the seed is said to strengthen memory, making it useful for study spells, and caraway is added to health and protection charms.
medicalUses: Like its cousins dill and fennel, caraway is a warming carminative used to relieve gas, colic, bloating and indigestion, often baked into heavy breads to make them easier to digest. Caraway seed tea or water was given to babies with wind and to adults with menstrual cramps, and caraway was used in cough syrups as a mild expectorant. The oil is part of some traditional digestive cordials such as kümmel.
whereToFind: Native to Europe, western Asia and North Africa; grows wild in meadows and roadsides in parts of northern Europe and is cultivated widely. Sow in spring in well-drained, sunny soil; it flowers in the second year, and seeds are harvested in summer when they darken. Caraway seed is sold in grocery spice aisles everywhere.
uses: Hide a few caraway seeds in your purse or car to protect against theft
Bake caraway seed cake to share with a lover for fidelity
Chew a few caraway seeds before study for a sharp memory
Add caraway to a love sachet with rose and cinnamon
Sprinkle caraway in a child's room (out of reach) for protection
Brew caraway seed tea to ease gas and bloating
Stir caraway into sauerkraut or rye bread as kitchen protection magic
caution: Safe in food amounts. Avoid medicinal doses of seed or oil in pregnancy (it may stimulate menstruation) and while breastfeeding. Caraway essential oil should not be taken internally except under professional guidance. May lower blood sugar; consult a healthcare provider if diabetic, and stop medicinal use 2 weeks before surgery. May increase iron absorption, so avoid extracts with hemochromatosis. Avoid if allergic to the carrot family.
interactions: May add to the effect of diabetes medicines and sedatives, may raise lithium levels, may lower potassium with diuretics, and may slow breakdown of some drugs processed by CYP1A1 (such as theophylline).

name: Coriander
description: Coriander is one of the oldest known spices: its seeds were found in the tomb of Tutankhamun and it is mentioned in the Bible, where manna is compared to coriander seed. The fresh leaves (cilantro) have a bright, divisive flavor while the round seeds are warm and citrusy. In the Arabian Nights it is an aphrodisiac, and Chinese tradition held that it conferred immortality.
metaphysicalUses: Coriander is a love herb of long standing: powdered seed is added to warm wine for a lust-stirring love potion, and seeds are carried in love sachets or added to love spells. It protects the home and its inhabitants when tied in a bundle and hung indoors, and brings peace to quarrelsome households. Coriander was believed to grant long life, and pregnant women in some traditions ate it so their children would be clever. Add it to healing incense, and bake coriander into bread for health and protection.
medicalUses: Coriander seed is a gentle, warming digestive used across Ayurvedic, Middle Eastern and European folk medicine for gas, bloating, indigestion and loss of appetite, often brewed as tea or taken in cooking. Ayurveda considers it cooling and uses coriander water for heat, burning urination and inflammation. Coriander poultices were used for rheumatic joints. The fresh leaf is eaten as a tonic food and traditionally used in heavy metal detoxification diets.
whereToFind: Native to southern Europe, North Africa and southwestern Asia; cultivated in gardens worldwide. Sow in cool weather in spring or autumn in sunny, well-drained soil; it bolts quickly in heat, and the flowers then set seed. Fresh cilantro and dried coriander seed are sold in every grocery store.
uses: Steep crushed coriander seed in warm wine for a sharing love potion
Hang a bundle of coriander in the home for protection and peace
Add coriander seed to a love sachet with rose petals
Bake coriander into bread as kitchen magic for health
Brew a coriander seed tea to settle indigestion
Toss coriander seeds into a ritual bath for healing and long life
caution: Generally safe in food amounts. Some people are allergic to coriander, especially those allergic to mugwort, aniseed, caraway, fennel, dill or other carrot-family plants; skin contact can irritate. Avoid medicinal amounts in pregnancy and breastfeeding. May lower blood sugar and blood pressure; consult a healthcare provider if taking related medications, and stop medicinal use 2 weeks before surgery.
interactions: In medicinal amounts may add to the effects of diabetes medicines, blood pressure medicines and sedatives.

name: Cumin
description: Cumin is a small, delicate annual whose warm, earthy, pungent seeds have seasoned food from ancient Egypt to India, Mexico and North Africa. In medieval Europe it was a symbol of fidelity: brides and grooms carried it through the ceremony, and soldiers were sent off with cumin-baked bread. Like caraway, it was believed to keep anything it touched from being stolen or straying.
metaphysicalUses: Cumin is a herb of fidelity and keeping. It was given to lovers and partners in food or wine to keep them faithful and to stoke lust, and it was carried by brides at weddings. Cumin seed is said to protect against theft when kept with belongings, and to keep chickens and pets from wandering. Burn cumin with frankincense for protection, or scatter it on the floor with salt to drive away evil. Cumin in the bath or sachet brings peace of mind, and some traditions use it to bind and hold a person or situation in place.
medicalUses: Cumin is a warming digestive spice used across many traditions to stimulate appetite, ease gas, bloating and colic, and settle indigestion and mild diarrhea. In Ayurveda, jeera water (cumin seeds steeped in hot water) is a gentle daily digestive and is given after childbirth. It was also used in traditional remedies for nausea and as a warming addition to food during colds.
whereToFind: Native to the eastern Mediterranean through to South Asia; cultivated in hot, dry regions including India, Iran, Syria, Turkey and Mexico. It needs a long, warm growing season and is harder to grow in cool climates. Whole and ground cumin seed is sold in every grocery store, and in bulk at Indian and Middle Eastern markets.
uses: Bake cumin into bread to share with a partner for fidelity
Scatter cumin and salt across the floor, then sweep out, to drive away evil
Burn cumin with frankincense for protection
Keep a sachet of cumin with valuables to guard against theft
Sip jeera water after meals to soothe digestion
Add cumin to a peace-of-mind bath sachet
caution: Safe in culinary amounts; some people are allergic to cumin. Avoid medicinal doses in pregnancy and while breastfeeding. Medicinal amounts may lower blood sugar and slow blood clotting, so consult a healthcare provider if you take diabetes or blood-thinning medication, and stop at least 2 weeks before surgery. Do not take cumin essential oil internally, and dilute it well on skin because it can cause sun sensitivity (phototoxicity). Burn incense on charcoal only in a well-ventilated room.
interactions: Medicinal amounts may add to the effects of diabetes medicines and blood thinners (anticoagulant and antiplatelet drugs), and may increase absorption of the antibiotic rifampin.

name: Black Pepper
description: Black pepper is the dried fruit of a climbing vine from the Malabar coast of India, once so precious that it was used as currency and ransom; Alaric the Goth demanded 3,000 pounds of it from Rome. Peppercorns were found stuffed in the nostrils of the mummy of Ramesses II. Hot, sharp and fiery, it brings Mars energy to any working.
metaphysicalUses: Black pepper is a fiery protector and banisher. Carry peppercorns in an amulet to free the mind of envious thoughts and to protect against the evil eye, or mix ground pepper with salt and scatter it around the property to dispel evil and keep unwanted people away. It is a key ingredient in banishing and hot-foot style workings, sprinkled where an unwanted person will walk, and added to uncrossing and hex-breaking spells to burn away negativity. Pepper also adds fire and speed to any spell and lends courage and determination.
medicalUses: Black pepper has been used in Ayurvedic and folk medicine as a warming digestive stimulant, encouraging appetite and the secretion of digestive juices and easing gas. Its heat was used in remedies for colds, coughs and congestion, often mixed with honey or ginger, and to warm cold extremities and improve circulation. Its compound piperine increases the absorption of other substances, which is why it is paired with turmeric.
whereToFind: Native to the Western Ghats of southern India; cultivated in tropical regions including India, Vietnam, Indonesia, Brazil and Sri Lanka. It can be grown as a houseplant in humid, warm conditions but rarely fruits indoors. Whole peppercorns are sold in every grocery store; buy whole and grind fresh for strongest effect.
uses: Mix black pepper and salt and sprinkle around your property to dispel evil
Carry whole peppercorns in a pouch to guard against envy
Add a pinch of black pepper to any spell to speed it up
Sprinkle black pepper in a banishing or hot-foot powder (never on skin)
Add peppercorns to a protective witch bottle
Brew pepper with ginger and honey as a warming cold-season drink
caution: Safe in food amounts. Large amounts can irritate the stomach and aggravate ulcers or reflux, and large amounts taken by mouth are likely unsafe in pregnancy. Inhaled or aspirated pepper has caused deaths in children; keep ground pepper and powders away from faces, children and pets. Piperine supplements (and very heavy pepper use) may slow clotting, lower blood sugar and raise blood levels of many drugs; consult a healthcare provider if taking medications, and stop supplement amounts 2 weeks before surgery. Do not apply undiluted black pepper oil to skin.
interactions: Piperine at supplement doses raises levels of carbamazepine, phenytoin, propranolol, theophylline, cyclosporine, lithium, fexofenadine, midazolam and other CYP3A4, CYP2D6 and P-glycoprotein substrates. May add to the effects of blood thinners (warfarin, aspirin, clopidogrel) and diabetes medicines.
pets: Keep ground pepper and hot-foot powders where pets cannot inhale or lick them.

name: Cayenne
description: Cayenne is the slender, scarlet chili pepper of the Americas, cultivated in Mexico for more than 6,000 years and named for the city of Cayenne in French Guiana. Its fierce heat comes from capsaicin, which the plant evolved to deter mammals. In folk magic, few herbs are hotter or more swift, and it is beloved in hoodoo for spells that need force and speed.
metaphysicalUses: Cayenne adds fire, speed and power to any spell. Scatter it around the house to break curses and prevent harm, or include it in a hot-foot powder to drive away an unwanted person. It is used to heat up a cold relationship, to spice love spells and to ensure faithfulness (sprinkled lightly under a partner's side of the rug in folk tradition), and to stir passion. Cayenne is also used in protection charms, in spells to overcome obstacles, and in 'hot' workings of domination and control. A dried pepper hung by the door wards off evil.
medicalUses: In folk and Physiomedical herbalism cayenne is a powerful circulatory stimulant, taken in small amounts in food, tea or tincture to warm the body, drive circulation to cold hands and feet, and support the system during colds and chills. Cayenne in honey and lemon was a traditional cold and sore throat remedy. Topically, capsaicin creams are used to ease arthritis, muscle pain and nerve pain, and a pinch of cayenne was famously sprinkled on minor cuts to stop bleeding, a practice not recommended today because it badly irritates broken skin.
whereToFind: Native to Central and South America and now cultivated worldwide in warm climates. Easy to grow as a sunny annual in gardens and pots; harvest when pods are red and dry them in strings (ristras). Ground cayenne is sold in every grocery store, and whole dried pods at Latin American and Asian markets.
uses: Scatter cayenne across the threshold (then sweep) to break a curse
Add a pinch of cayenne to any spell to speed it up and give it force
Hang a string of dried red chilies by the door to ward off evil
Sprinkle cayenne in a hot-foot powder to drive away an unwanted person
Add a pinch to honey and lemon for a warming cold remedy
Use a capsaicin salve on aching joints (external, wash hands after)
caution: Very irritating to eyes, mucous membranes and broken skin; wear gloves, wash hands thoroughly and never touch your face after handling, and work with fresh air because the fumes can trigger asthma. Do not apply to wounds or near eyes, do not use heating pads over capsaicin cream, and patch test topical preparations. Can aggravate ulcers, reflux and IBS, and large amounts may raise blood pressure. Avoid medicinal amounts in pregnancy and breastfeeding (rashes have occurred in nursing infants). Keep powders away from children and pets.
interactions: May increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs (warfarin, apixaban, aspirin, clopidogrel) and with garlic, ginger or ginkgo supplements. Topical capsaicin may worsen ACE inhibitor cough; oral cayenne may raise theophylline absorption, affect blood pressure medicines, and should be avoided with cyclosporine.
pets: Powder and sprays are highly irritating to pets' eyes, noses and stomachs.

name: Mustard Seed
description: Mustard is a fast-growing, yellow-flowered brassica whose tiny seeds hold astonishing heat and life; in the Gospel parable the smallest of seeds grows into a tree where birds may nest. Pope John XXII was said to love mustard so much he created the office of 'Grand Mustard-Maker to the Pope'. In folk magic the seed is a symbol of faith, fertility and confusion for one's enemies.
metaphysicalUses: Carry a single mustard seed in a small vial or locket as a talisman of faith, luck and the power to move mountains; wearing it also increases fertility. Black mustard seed is a classic hoodoo ingredient for confusing enemies and causing quarrels between those who would harm you, and it is scattered in doorways or buried under the doorstep to keep supernatural beings away. Mustard seeds are also laid along windowsills and thresholds because spirits are compelled to count them before passing. Eaten in food or carried, mustard lends mental courage and strength.
medicalUses: Mustard has been used chiefly as a warming external remedy: the mustard plaster or poultice, a paste of ground seed and flour wrapped in cloth, was laid on the chest for congestion, bronchitis and chest colds, and on aching muscles and stiff joints to bring warmth and circulation. Hot mustard footbaths were used to relieve head colds and chilblains. Taken in food it stimulates digestion and appetite.
whereToFind: Native to the Mediterranean, North Africa and temperate Asia and naturalized widely as a field weed and on roadsides. Easy to grow as a quick annual in spring or autumn. Black, brown and yellow mustard seed is sold in grocery stores, Indian markets and spice shops; hoodoo shops stock black mustard seed specifically.
uses: Wear a single mustard seed in a locket as a talisman of faith and luck
Scatter black mustard seed in an enemy's path to confuse them (in folk tradition)
Lay a line of mustard seeds on the windowsill so spirits must stop to count them
Bury mustard seed beneath the doorstep to keep unwanted beings away
Make a traditional mustard plaster for chest congestion (short time, external)
Add a pinch to a fertility charm bag
caution: Mustard plasters and poultices can burn and blister the skin; place a cloth between the paste and skin, check often, never leave on more than 15-20 minutes, and never use on children, sensitive or broken skin. Avoid mustard essential oil entirely; its allyl isothiocyanate is a strong irritant, and mustard oil should not be massaged on newborns. Mustard is a common food allergen. Large internal doses can damage the throat and stomach. Avoid more than food amounts in pregnancy (medicinal amounts may cause miscarriage) and when breastfeeding, and with thyroid conditions.
interactions: Medicinal amounts may lower blood sugar and add to the effect of diabetes medicines.

name: Bayberry
description: Bayberry is an aromatic evergreen shrub of the eastern American coast whose small grey berries are coated in a fragrant wax. Colonial families boiled the berries to skim off the wax and made greenish, spicy-scented candles, a laborious craft that made them precious. From this grew the New England saying, 'A bayberry candle burned to the socket brings food to the larder and gold to the pocket.'
metaphysicalUses: Bayberry is the money-drawing herb of the American folk tradition. A bayberry candle is lit on Christmas Eve or New Year's Eve and allowed to burn completely down to bring luck, money and abundance for the year ahead, and it is burned in prosperity and success rites year round. The root bark is added to money-drawing powders, oils and sachets, and bayberry brings peace, harmony and well-being to the home. Gifting a bayberry candle is a blessing of good fortune for the household.
