medicalUses: Bayberry root bark was a cornerstone of Samuel Thomson's 19th-century American folk medicine. As a strong astringent and warming stimulant, it was used as a gargle for sore throats and spongy, bleeding gums, taken in small doses for diarrhea and colds, and was a key ingredient in the famous 'Composition Powder' given to bring on a sweat at the onset of a chill.
whereToFind: Native to eastern North America, from New Jersey down the Atlantic and Gulf coasts to Texas and the Caribbean, growing in coastal sand dunes, pine barrens, swamps and wet woods; northern bayberry (Morella pensylvanica) grows further north. Berries are harvested in autumn. Plants are sold at native nurseries; bayberry candles, wax and root bark from candle makers and herb or hoodoo shops.
uses: Burn a bayberry candle all the way down on New Year's Eve for a prosperous year
Give a bayberry candle as a blessing for a new home
Add bayberry root bark to a money-drawing sachet or powder
Dress a green candle with bayberry oil for business success
Plant a wax myrtle near the house for harmony and abundance
Use a bayberry bark gargle for sore gums (spit out)
caution: Bayberry bark is considered possibly unsafe internally: it can cause nausea, vomiting and liver damage, and its tannins caused cancer in animal studies, so use the gargle only and spit it out. Avoid entirely in pregnancy and breastfeeding, and with high blood pressure, heart conditions or kidney disease (it can cause sodium and fluid retention). Never leave a burning candle unattended.
interactions: May interfere with blood pressure medicines and may affect drugs processed by CYP3A4 and CYP2C9 liver enzymes.

name: Allspice
description: Allspice is the dried berry of a tropical evergreen tree of the Caribbean and Central America, so named by the English because it tastes like a blend of cinnamon, clove and nutmeg. The Maya used it in embalming, and it is the heart of Jamaican jerk seasoning. Its warm, sweet-spicy scent is the very smell of good fortune in folk tradition.
metaphysicalUses: Allspice is burned as an incense or added to sachets and mixtures to attract money and luck, and to bring a swift, determined energy to spells. It lends a boost of energy and willpower to any working, and is added to healing mixtures and to blends that help achieve one's goals. Carry allspice berries in a pouch for good fortune, add them to a prosperity jar, or put a few in a business till to draw customers and success. Allspice is also used in Mars workings to overcome obstacles.
medicalUses: Like clove, allspice contains eugenol, and in Caribbean and Central American folk medicine it was used as a warming digestive for gas, indigestion and colic, a poultice or rub for aching muscles and rheumatism, and a remedy for toothache. Allspice tea was drunk to warm the body during colds and chills.
whereToFind: Native to Jamaica, the Greater Antilles, southern Mexico and Central America, growing in lowland tropical forest; cultivated mainly in Jamaica. It needs a frost-free climate but can be grown as a potted indoor tree in cool regions. Whole and ground allspice is sold in every grocery store; buy whole berries for spell work.
uses: Burn crushed allspice on charcoal as a money-drawing incense
Carry seven allspice berries in a green pouch for luck
Add allspice berries to a prosperity jar with cinnamon and bay leaf
Place a few berries in your cash register to draw customers
Add allspice to a determination spell to see a goal through
Simmer allspice with orange peel as a prosperity stovetop potpourri
caution: Safe in culinary amounts. The essential oil is a skin and mucous membrane irritant: keep it to no more than about 0.15% on skin (about 1 drop per 30 ml of carrier oil), never use it in the bath, and do not take it internally; swallowing more than a few milliliters of the oil can cause vomiting and seizures. Eugenol may slow blood clotting, so use caution with blood thinners and before surgery. Avoid medicinal doses in pregnancy. Burn incense on charcoal only in a well-ventilated room.
interactions: Medicinal amounts or the oil may add to the effects of blood thinners and antiplatelet drugs.
pets: Keep allspice oil away from cats.

name: Cardamom
description: Cardamom is the Queen of Spices, the aromatic seed pod of a lush ginger-family plant from the rainforests of southern India. Its sweet, eucalyptus-bright perfume scents chai, Arabic coffee and Scandinavian buns alike, and it was carried along ancient caravan routes as a luxury. The Arabian Nights name it an aphrodisiac, and it has long been chewed to sweeten the breath before a kiss.
metaphysicalUses: Cardamom is a love and lust herb: ground cardamom is added to warmed wine or tea for a quick love potion, baked into apple pie or pastries for kitchen love magic, and added to sachets and incense to bring love and passion. It also lifts the spirits, brings clarity of thought and courage, and smooths communication, so it is used in spells for heartfelt conversation and harmony between partners. Chewing a pod before speaking sweetens words as well as breath.
medicalUses: Cardamom is a warming, aromatic digestive in Ayurvedic and Middle Eastern folk medicine, used to ease nausea, gas, bloating and indigestion and to stimulate the appetite. Chewing the seeds freshens the breath and was a traditional after-meal custom. It was added to milk and coffee to make them easier to digest, and used in remedies for coughs and colds.
whereToFind: Native to the Western Ghats of southern India; cultivated in India, Sri Lanka, Guatemala and Tanzania in shady, humid tropical forest. It can be grown as a leafy houseplant in cool climates, though it rarely fruits indoors. Green cardamom pods and ground cardamom are sold in grocery stores and in bulk at Indian and Middle Eastern markets.
uses: Stir ground cardamom into warm wine or chai as a love potion
Bake cardamom into buns or apple pie for kitchen love magic
Chew a pod before a heartfelt conversation to sweeten your words
Add cardamom pods to a love sachet with rose and vanilla
Burn cardamom in incense for clarity and lifted spirits
Sip cardamom tea after meals to settle digestion
caution: Safe in normal food amounts. People with gallstones should avoid amounts larger than those used to flavor food, because cardamom seed can trigger gallstone colic (spasmodic pain). Its safety in medicinal amounts during pregnancy and breastfeeding is unknown, so stick to food amounts. Dilute the essential oil well for skin use (about 1%) and do not take the oil internally; keep it away from children's faces.
interactions: No well-documented drug interactions at food amounts. Ask a doctor before taking cardamom supplements alongside regular medicines.
pets: Keep cardamom essential oil away from cats and do not diffuse it in small closed rooms with pets.

name: Vanilla
description: Vanilla is the fragrant cured pod of a climbing orchid native to Mexico, whose pale flowers open for only a single day. The Totonac people tell that it sprang from the blood of the princess Xanath and her mortal lover, and the Aztecs flavored their chocolate with it. It is the second most expensive spice in the world, for every flower must be pollinated by hand.
metaphysicalUses: Vanilla is one of the sweetest herbs of love and allure. A vanilla bean placed in a jar of sugar infuses the sugar with love vibrations for use in love spells and sweetening jars, and the scent of vanilla oil or extract, dabbed on the pulse points, draws love and desire. Carry a bean to restore lost energy and improve the mind, add it to love sachets and honey jars, and use it in self-love baths to feel beautiful and beloved. Its warm comfort also brings happiness, calm and sweet memories, and it is used to sweeten someone toward you.
medicalUses: Vanilla is primarily a flavoring, but in folk use it was considered a gentle calming and comforting scent, inhaled to ease anxiety and stress, and taken in warm milk to soothe the stomach and encourage sleep. In Mexican tradition it was regarded as a mild aphrodisiac and tonic. Its aroma remains one of the most comforting in aromatherapy.
whereToFind: Native to the tropical forests of southeastern Mexico and Central America; cultivated in Madagascar, Réunion, Tahiti, Indonesia, Uganda and Mexico. It can be grown as a climbing orchid in a warm, humid greenhouse but rarely flowers in homes. Whole vanilla beans, pure extract and vanilla absolute are sold in grocery stores, baking shops and aromatherapy suppliers.
uses: Bury a vanilla bean in a jar of sugar to make love-charged sugar for sweetening spells
Dab a little pure vanilla extract on your pulse points to attract love
Add a vanilla bean to a honey jar to sweeten someone toward you
Carry a vanilla bean in your pocket to restore energy and lift the mind
Add vanilla to a self-love ritual bath with rose petals
Steep a vanilla pod in warm milk for a comforting bedtime drink
caution: Generally very safe as food; stick to food amounts in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Vanilla extract contains alcohol; do not give large amounts to children. Some people are sensitive to vanilla on the skin; patch test before applying extract or absolute. Avoid cheap 'Mexican vanilla' made with tonka bean: the FDA bans coumarin from US food, and it is toxic to the liver in high doses and may increase bleeding with blood thinners. Check labels for 'vanilla bean' and buy reputable pure vanilla.
interactions: Coumarin-adulterated vanilla may add to the effect of warfarin and other blood thinners.
pets: Vanilla extract is high in alcohol; keep it away from dogs and cats.

name: Orange Peel
description: The orange is a little captured sun, its glowing peel full of bright, uplifting oils. Some scholars think the golden apples of the Hesperides that Hera received as a wedding gift were oranges, and brides have long worn orange blossom for fertility and happiness. Dried orange peel is a staple of Chinese medicine and of witches' cupboards alike.
metaphysicalUses: Orange peel is a herb of joy, luck and abundance. Add dried peel to love sachets and incense, to prosperity and money powders, and to solar spells for success and vitality; it is the bright note in many Sun and Lammas blends. Drinking orange-peel tea or juice is said to bring happiness and love, and orange blossom added to the bath makes one more attractive. An old divination asks a question while eating an orange: count the seeds, an even number answers no, an odd number yes. Orange peel is also used in purification and to lift the energy of a gloomy home.
medicalUses: Dried orange and tangerine peel (chen pi) is an ancient digestive in Chinese and European folk medicine, brewed as tea to ease bloating, gas, nausea and poor appetite and to help clear phlegm from coughs. Its bright scent has long been used to lift low mood and ease nervous tension, and orange blossom water was a gentle calming remedy for children and adults.
whereToFind: Native to southern China and Southeast Asia and now cultivated in warm climates worldwide, from Spain and Morocco to Florida, California and Brazil. Grow dwarf oranges in pots that winter indoors in cool climates. Save peels from organic oranges, scrape off the white pith and dry them in a low oven or warm place. Dried peel is also sold at spice shops and herb suppliers.
uses: Dry organic orange peel and add it to money and prosperity sachets
Simmer orange peel with cinnamon and clove for a joyful home-blessing potpourri
Count the seeds of an orange to answer a yes-or-no question
Add orange peel to sun magic and Litha or Lammas incense
Brew a tea of dried peel to ease bloating
Add orange blossom water to a love bath for attraction
caution: Sweet orange peel and oil are not considered phototoxic, but they can irritate skin, and old or oxidized citrus oil can cause skin allergy; always dilute. Bitter orange (Citrus aurantium) oil is phototoxic, so avoid sun for 12 hours after applying it, and its peel or extract contains stimulants: avoid it with heart conditions, high blood pressure, and in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Use organic fruit or wash well to avoid pesticide residue.
interactions: Bitter orange extracts may add to the effects of stimulants and caffeine and have been linked to heart problems in combination products; ask a provider if you take any medicine.
pets: Citrus essential oils are toxic to cats; do not diffuse or apply them around cats.

name: Lemon
description: The lemon is a fruit of brightness and clearing, its sharp, clean scent cutting through stale air and stale energy alike. Probably native to the foothills of the Himalayas, it traveled through Persia and the Arab world to the Mediterranean. Sailors carried it against scurvy, and in folk magic it is the great purifier and the key ingredient of countless cleansing washes.
metaphysicalUses: Lemon is the witch's purifier. Lemon juice mixed with water is used to wash amulets, jewelry and magical tools to cleanse them of past influences, and is added to floor washes and full-moon baths for purification and uncrossing. Dried lemon blossom and peel are added to love sachets, and lemon leaves to friendship spells; serving a guest a slice of lemon pie is said to strengthen their friendship and fidelity. A lemon studded with pins (with colored heads) and hung by the door protects the home, and lemon is used in spells to cut ties, sour a situation or end a hex. It is a Moon herb, cleansing and clarifying.
medicalUses: Hot water with lemon and honey is perhaps the best known folk remedy of all, sipped to soothe sore throats and support the body through colds. Lemon's vitamin C made it the classic remedy for scurvy. Lemon juice in warm water was taken in the morning to stimulate digestion, and diluted juice was used as a mild astringent on oily skin.
whereToFind: Probably native to northeast India and northern Myanmar; cultivated in warm, frost-free regions including the Mediterranean, California, Mexico and Argentina. Dwarf Meyer lemons grow well in large pots brought indoors in winter. Lemons are sold year-round in every grocery store; choose organic if using the peel.
uses: Wash crystals and magical tools in lemon water to cleanse old energies
Add lemon juice to a floor wash for purification and uncrossing
Serve lemon pie to a friend to strengthen your friendship
Add dried lemon peel to a full-moon cleansing bath
Use a halved lemon in a cord-cutting or souring spell
Sip hot water with lemon and honey to soothe a sore throat
caution: Cold-pressed lemon essential oil and lemon juice on skin can cause burns and dark patches in sunlight; avoid sun for 12-18 hours after topical use, and never apply undiluted essential oil. Steam-distilled lemon oil is not phototoxic. Acidic juice can erode tooth enamel (rinse after drinking) and irritate reflux or mouth ulcers. Generally safe as food. Honey in lemon drinks must not be given to babies under 1 year.
interactions: Lemon juice may lower chloroquine levels and increases iron absorption.
pets: Lemon peel, plant and citrus essential oils are toxic to dogs, cats and horses (vomiting, diarrhea, depression, skin irritation); do not diffuse or apply them around cats.

name: Apple
description: The apple is the fruit of love, wisdom and the Otherworld. Cut it crosswise and its seeds form a five-pointed star, the witch's pentagram. Avalon, the Isle of Apples, was where Arthur was carried to heal, the Norse gods stayed young eating Idunna's golden apples, and a silver bough of apple was the passport into the faery realm in Irish myth. At Samhain apples are food for the dead.
metaphysicalUses: The apple is a love fruit above all: share an apple with someone you love to bind your affection, or cut an apple in half, give half to your beloved and eat the other half. Apple blossoms are added to love sachets and incense, and apple cider replaces blood or wine in some ritual. At Samhain, apples are buried in the earth or left on the altar as food for the departed and for spirits who have not yet been reborn, and apple divinations abound: peel an apple in one long strip and throw it over your shoulder to see the initial of your future love, or bob for apples. Apple wood makes wands for love and healing, and the star within is used in pentacle magic.
medicalUses: 'An apple a day keeps the doctor away' sums up the folk wisdom. Raw grated apple was a traditional remedy for diarrhea thanks to its pectin, while baked apples and stewed apples eased constipation. Apple cider vinegar has been taken diluted as a folk tonic for digestion. Apples are nourishing for the heart and digestion, and apple-leaf poultices were occasionally laid on bruises.
whereToFind: The domestic apple descends from wild apples of the Tian Shan mountains of Kazakhstan; crab apples grow wild in hedgerows and woodland edges across Europe and North America. Apple trees are grown in orchards and gardens throughout temperate regions and are sold at nurseries. Blossoms appear in spring; harvest fruit in late summer and autumn. Dried apple blossom is sold by some herb suppliers.
uses: Cut an apple crosswise to reveal the pentagram and use it as an offering
Share an apple with your beloved to bind your love
Peel an apple in one strip and toss it over your shoulder to divine your love's initial
Bury an apple at Samhain as food for wandering spirits and ancestors
Cut an apple-wood wand for love and healing magic
Simmer apple cider with cinnamon for a Mabon or Samhain ritual drink
Add dried apple blossoms to love incense
caution: The fruit is safe and wholesome. Apple seeds contain amygdalin, which releases cyanide when crushed or chewed; swallowing the seeds in a core is not dangerous, but do not chew or grind large amounts of seeds. Leaves and bark should not be ingested. Some people have apple allergies linked to birch pollen.
interactions: Apple juice can sharply reduce absorption of some drugs, including fexofenadine, atenolol and aliskiren; take these with water, not apple juice.
pets: Apple stems, leaves and seeds contain cyanide-forming compounds and are toxic to dogs, cats and horses; remove cores before sharing fruit.

name: Pomegranate
description: The pomegranate is a jewel box of a fruit, its leathery red rind hiding hundreds of glistening ruby seeds. In the Greek myth Persephone ate six pomegranate seeds in the underworld and so must return to Hades for six months each year, bringing winter to the land. A symbol of fertility, abundance and the mysteries of death and rebirth, it was carved on the pillars of Solomon's temple.
metaphysicalUses: Pomegranate is sacred to the underworld goddess and to fertility. Eat the seeds to increase fertility, and always make a wish before eating a pomegranate, for it will come true. The juice can be used in place of blood or as an ink for spells, and the dried rind is added to wealth and abundance spells. A branch of pomegranate was used as a divining rod for hidden treasure and wealth. Offer pomegranates to Persephone and the ancestors at Samhain and the autumn equinox, and use the fruit in shadow work and descent rituals to honor the cycle of death and return.
medicalUses: The fruit and juice are a nourishing, antioxidant-rich food traditionally used to support the heart and circulation. The astringent rind was used in Middle Eastern and Ayurvedic folk medicine as a decoction for diarrhea and as a gargle for sore throats and mouth sores. The root and stem bark were historically used against intestinal worms, but are toxic in excess and not used at home.
whereToFind: Native to Iran and the region to northern India, and cultivated since ancient times throughout the Mediterranean, Middle East, India, California and the American Southwest. It grows as a shrub or small tree in hot, dry summers and is sold at nurseries in warmer zones. Fruit is in season in autumn and early winter in grocery stores; dried rind is sold by herb and Middle Eastern shops.
uses: Make a wish before eating pomegranate seeds
Eat six seeds at Samhain in honor of Persephone and the descent into winter
Use pomegranate juice as a ritual ink for writing petitions
Offer a split pomegranate on the ancestor altar
Add dried pomegranate rind to an abundance and wealth sachet
Share pomegranate seeds with a partner in a fertility rite
caution: The fruit and juice are safe as food; diarrhea and allergic reactions are occasionally reported. Pomegranate juice may increase bleeding risk with warfarin, and people on statins, blood pressure medicines or diabetes medicines (the juice is sugary) should consult a healthcare provider. The root, stem, bark and peel contain harmful compounds and should not be ingested in large amounts at home.
interactions: A case report links regular juice to a raised INR on warfarin; use caution with warfarin and other anticoagulants. Animal studies suggest CYP3A and CYP2C9 inhibition, though human studies have not shown a clinically relevant effect. May increase rhabdomyolysis risk with statins.

name: Raspberry Leaf
description: Raspberry is a bramble of the woodland edge whose soft red fruit has been gathered since the Stone Age. Its Latin name idaeus recalls Mount Ida, where legend says the nymph Ida pricked her finger picking white berries for the infant Zeus and stained them red forever. The leaves are the classic 'woman's herb', a tonic for the womb drunk by generations of midwives' clients.
metaphysicalUses: Raspberry brambles are hung at the door and in windows to keep unwanted spirits from entering, and in old custom the canes were hung up at funerals and at the house of the dead so the spirit would not return. Raspberry leaf is a herb of the feminine, used in fertility charms, rituals of motherhood and childbirth, and spells for a woman's health and protection. The fruit is served as a love food, eaten together to induce love and passion, and raspberry leaf in the bath encourages happiness and self-love.
medicalUses: Raspberry leaf tea is a traditional uterine tonic, drunk in the later stages of pregnancy (under midwife guidance) to prepare and tone the womb for labor, and during menstruation to ease cramping and heavy periods. Being astringent and rich in minerals, it was also used for diarrhea, as a gargle for sore throats and mouth ulcers, and as a wash for minor wounds.
whereToFind: Native to Europe and northern Asia, with closely related species across North America; grows wild in woodland clearings, hedgerows and burned or disturbed ground and is cultivated widely in gardens. Harvest leaves before or during flowering in late spring and early summer, and dry them thoroughly. Dried leaf is sold by herb suppliers and health food stores.
uses: Hang a raspberry cane over the door to keep unwanted spirits out
Drink raspberry leaf tea in rituals honoring motherhood and the feminine
Share fresh raspberries with a lover to induce passion
Add raspberry leaf to a fertility charm bag
Brew raspberry leaf tea to ease menstrual cramping
Add raspberry leaf to a self-love bath with rose
caution: Do not use in early pregnancy; use in later pregnancy only with the approval and supervision of your midwife or healthcare provider, as it may stimulate uterine contractions. Avoid while breastfeeding and with estrogen-sensitive conditions such as breast, uterine or ovarian cancer, endometriosis or fibroids. Leaves must be fully dried before use (wilting leaves can cause nausea). May add to the effect of diabetes medications.
interactions: May enhance the blood-sugar-lowering effect of diabetes medicines.

name: Blackberry
description: The blackberry bramble scrambles thorny and unstoppable through hedges and waste ground, offering sweet dark berries at summer's end. British folklore warns never to pick blackberries after Michaelmas, the 29th of September, or the 10th of October in old reckoning, for on that day the Devil, cast out of Heaven into a bramble, spits on them. Brambles were planted on graves to keep the dead within.
metaphysicalUses: Blackberry is a protection and abundance plant. The thorny canes are used in protective spells and planted on boundaries and graves to keep out intruders and keep the restless dead from walking; a sprig hung by the door wards off evil. Blackberry leaves are used in money and prosperity spells, and blackberry pie is baked at Lughnasadh to celebrate the harvest and welcome abundance. Passing a sick child or adult beneath an arching bramble that had rooted at both ends was an old healing charm. Brambles are also used in binding magic, and the berries are offered to the fair folk and to Brigid.
medicalUses: Blackberry leaf and root are strongly astringent, and their tea or decoction is a gentle, time-honored remedy for diarrhea, especially in children, and a gargle for sore throats, bleeding gums and mouth ulcers. The leaves were chewed for bleeding gums and laid on minor wounds and scalds. The berries are rich in vitamins and were made into cordials for colds and anemia.
whereToFind: Native across Europe and naturalized (often invasively) in North America, Australia and elsewhere; grows in hedgerows, woodland edges, waste ground, railway banks and abandoned fields. Pick leaves in spring and early summer, berries from late July to September (before Michaelmas), and roots in autumn. Wear long sleeves for the thorns. Dried blackberry leaf is sold by herb suppliers.
uses: Plant blackberry along your boundary as a thorny protective hedge
Bake blackberry pie at Lughnasadh to honor the harvest
Add dried blackberry leaves to a money-drawing sachet
Weave a bramble cane into a protective wreath for the door
Leave a bowl of blackberries for the fair folk
Brew blackberry leaf tea to calm an upset tummy with diarrhea
Use a blackberry leaf gargle for a sore throat
caution: Generally safe. Leaves and root are high in tannins; avoid long-term or heavy internal use, and consult a healthcare provider in pregnancy. Use only fully dried or fresh leaves (wilting leaves can cause stomach upset). Seek medical advice for diarrhea lasting more than a couple of days, especially in children. Beware of thorns, and do not forage near sprayed roadsides.
interactions: Tannins may reduce absorption of other medicines; take at a different time.

name: Strawberry
description: The tiny wild strawberry creeps through woodland glades, its little heart-shaped red fruits dotted with seeds and fragrant beyond any garden berry. To the Romans it was sacred to Venus, and for its heart shape and red color it became a fruit of love. In Norse lore Frigga hid the souls of dead children in strawberries to smuggle them into heaven. The Haudenosaunee celebrate the first fruits of the year at the Strawberry Festival.
metaphysicalUses: Strawberries are a fruit of love: serve them to a beloved to arouse love, share a double strawberry with someone so you will fall in love, and carry or add the leaves to love sachets. Strawberry leaves are also carried for luck, and pregnant women were advised to carry a pouch of the leaves to ease the pains of pregnancy. The berries are offered to the fair folk and to love goddesses, used in beauty and glamour spells, and eaten at Midsummer and Beltane to celebrate the sweetness of life. Strawberry leaf in a bath brings happiness and friendship.
medicalUses: Wild strawberry leaf, like raspberry and blackberry, is mildly astringent and was brewed as a gentle tea for mild diarrhea and as a gargle for sore gums and mouth ulcers. It was considered a mild diuretic and a nourishing tonic tea. The crushed fruit was rubbed on teeth to whiten them and applied to the face as a mask for sunburn and skin blemishes; Linnaeus claimed strawberries cured his gout.
whereToFind: Wild strawberry is native across much of the Northern Hemisphere, in woodland clearings, hedgebanks, meadows and grassy slopes; garden strawberries (Fragaria x ananassa) are grown everywhere. Gather leaves in spring and summer, fruits in early to midsummer. Plants are sold at garden centers; dried leaf from herbal suppliers.
uses: Share a double strawberry with someone to kindle love
Serve strawberries and cream at a Midsummer or Beltane celebration
Carry a pouch of strawberry leaves for good luck
Leave a few wild strawberries in the woods as an offering to the fair folk
Add strawberry leaves to a love sachet with rose and vanilla
Make a gentle strawberry leaf tea for an upset stomach
Mash strawberries into a beauty face mask for glamour magic
caution: Strawberries are a common allergen and can cause hives, itching or swelling of the mouth in sensitive people, especially those allergic to birch pollen; rarely, reactions are severe. Use only fully dried or fresh leaves (wilting leaves can cause upset). Avoid medicinal amounts of leaf in pregnancy without consulting a healthcare provider. Choose organic fruit to avoid pesticide residue.

name: Catnip
description: Catnip is a soft, grey-green mint with spikes of pale lilac-spotted flowers that sends cats into ecstasy with its compound nepetalactone. It is sacred to the cat goddess Bast, and old witches grew it to delight their familiars. In English folk practice its root was chewed by hangmen before work to make them fierce, while its leaves were brewed into a gentle calming tea for children.
metaphysicalUses: Catnip is a herb of feline magic, love and happiness. Give it to your cat to create a psychic bond with your familiar, and use it in spells honoring Bast. Catnip is added to love sachets, especially with rose petals, and holding catnip in your hand until it is warm, then holding the hand of another, ensures their friendship forever; keep the leaf in a safe place. Large catnip leaves are pressed and used as bookmarks in magical books. Grown near the home or hung over the door, it draws good spirits and luck, and it is used in dream pillows and calming spells to bring peace and happiness.
medicalUses: Catnip tea is one of the gentlest calming herbs of folk medicine: a mild relaxant for nervous tension, restlessness and sleeplessness, and a soothing digestive for colic, gas and upset stomach, traditionally given in small amounts to children (modern references advise against giving it to children by mouth). Hot catnip tea was used to bring on a gentle sweat to break a fever during colds and flu. Crushed leaves were rubbed on the skin as a mild insect repellent.
whereToFind: Native to Europe, the Middle East and central Asia and naturalized across North America; grows in dry, sunny, disturbed places, field edges, roadsides and old gardens. Very easy to grow (you may need to guard it from cats). Harvest leaves and flowering tops in summer. Dried catnip is sold at herb shops and in every pet store.
uses: Give your cat catnip to deepen the bond with your familiar
Add catnip and rose petals to a love sachet
Warm catnip in your palm, then hold a friend's hand to seal a friendship
Use a pressed catnip leaf as a bookmark in your grimoire
Sew catnip into a dream pillow for peaceful, happy dreams
Brew a cup of catnip tea before bed to unwind
Plant catnip by the door to draw good spirits and luck
caution: Avoid in pregnancy (it may stimulate the uterus) and breastfeeding, and with heavy menstrual bleeding or pelvic inflammatory disease. May cause drowsiness, especially with sedatives or alcohol; do not drive after use, and stop 2 weeks before surgery. Large amounts can cause vomiting. Not recommended for infants or children by mouth. Generally safe for cats, though some may overindulge.
interactions: May add to drowsiness with sedatives (benzodiazepines, barbiturates, sleep aids, sedating antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants) and may raise lithium levels.
pets: Safe for most cats, but too much can cause vomiting or diarrhea.

name: Damiana
description: Damiana is a small aromatic shrub of the dry hills of Mexico and Central America, with fig-scented leaves and little yellow flowers. The Maya and later Mexican folk healers used it as a tonic and aphrodisiac, and it is the flavor of a traditional Mexican liqueur sold in a bottle shaped like a goddess. In modern witchcraft it is beloved for lust, visions and opening the psychic eye.
metaphysicalUses: Damiana is a herb of passion and of vision. Brewed as a tea or burned as incense, it is used in lust spells to awaken desire and bring passion into a relationship, and it is included in love sachets and charm bags. Burned as incense or drunk before divination, it is said to enhance psychic visions, scrying and trance work, and it is a common ingredient in visionary and sex magic blends. Damiana also lends energy and sensual vitality to self-love and attraction workings.
medicalUses: In Mexican folk medicine damiana is a warming, uplifting tonic, taken as a tea or liqueur to lift low mood, ease mild anxiety and nervous exhaustion, support digestion and, traditionally, as an aphrodisiac to restore libido and vitality in both men and women. It was also used as a mild urinary antiseptic.
whereToFind: Native to southern Texas, Mexico, Central and South America and the Caribbean, growing in dry, rocky, sunny hillsides and scrub. It is rarely grown outside warm climates but can be kept as a potted shrub. Dried damiana leaf is sold by herbal apothecaries, metaphysical shops and online suppliers; damiana liqueur at liquor stores.
uses: Brew damiana tea to share with a partner in a lust spell
Burn damiana as an incense before scrying or tarot to enhance visions
Add damiana to a red charm bag for passion and attraction
Infuse damiana in brandy with honey for a love cordial
Add damiana to a sensual self-love ritual bath
Blend damiana with mugwort in a visionary dream incense
caution: Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding (it contains cyanogenic glycosides that may be toxic at high doses). May lower blood sugar; consult a healthcare provider if diabetic or taking diabetes medication, and stop two weeks before surgery. Very large doses may cause convulsions, especially with heavy alcohol use; do not combine with alcohol or drive after large amounts. Claims of hallucinogenic effects are not supported. Burn as incense only with good ventilation.
interactions: May add to the effect of diabetes medicines (insulin, metformin, sulfonylureas), causing low blood sugar.
